places.name: Mangaluru (Mangalore)
places.summary: Karnataka's old port city on the Arabian Sea — Kadri temple, Sultan Battery, painted chapels and famous fish curry.
places.seoDescription: Mangaluru: the old port of Mangalapura — Kadri Manjunath Temple, Sultan Battery, St Aloysius Chapel's frescoes, neer dosa and fish curry.

images.alt: The wide sands of Panambur Beach, Mangaluru
images.caption: Panambur Beach, Mangaluru

overview.text:
Mangaluru — still often called Mangalore — sits on Karnataka's coast where rivers meet the Arabian Sea, and it has been a port for centuries. As 'Mangalapura' it traded with Arabia, Persia and Europe, and in the 16th century Vasco da Gama landed here, beginning the Portuguese chapter of its history.

That mix shows today. Tulu, Konkani, Kannada and Malayalam are all spoken, and the city's sights range from the 10th-century Kadri Manjunath Temple, with its carvings and sacred tank, to St Aloysius Chapel, covered in frescoes, and Sultan Battery, Tipu Sultan's watchtower over the sea. Come hungry: Mangaluru is famous for neer dosa and Mangalorean fish curry. It is also the gateway to Kudremukh and Kodachadri in the Western Ghats.

items.body: Visit the 10th-century Kadri Manjunath Temple and its sacred tank.
See the frescoes of St Aloysius Chapel.
Look out over the sea from Sultan Battery.

Mangalorean fish curry.

images.alt: Rolling green hills of Kudremukh under cloud
images.caption: Kudremukh

overview.text:
Kudremukh National Park protects more than 600 sq km of the Western Ghats, and its landscape is one of the most beautiful in Karnataka: rolling green grassland folded around patches of dark shola forest, with rainforest in the valleys and mist drifting over the peaks.

Most people come to walk. The trek to Kudremukh Peak is the classic, climbing through the grassland ridges for wide views; the Bhagavathi Nature Camp is a gentler base in the forest. Elephants and tigers live in the park, along with a wealth of orchids and tall trees. The park is open from 10 am to 5 pm. Combine it with Sringeri, the historic temple town about 60 km away.

overview.text:
Kodachadri is a peak of the Western Ghats rising to about 1,343 m, its slopes covered in forest and grass and often wrapped in cloud. The name is said to mean "jasmine of the hills", and the place carries a long history: it is tied to the Kadamba dynasty and is said to have sheltered Queen Chennamma of Keladi in her fight against colonial forces.

At the very top stands a small stone temple to Mookambika, the spiritual heart of the hill, built in a plain style that fits the rough landscape. The walk along the ridge gives huge views over the Ghats. Kollur's famous Mookambika Temple is about 20 km away, and the old walls of Nagara Fort are about 4 miles from the hill.

overview.text:
Vijayapura — long known as Bijapur — lies in the north of the Karnataka plateau and was one of the great cities of the Deccan from the late 15th to the late 17th century. Its sultans left behind a skyline of domes and minarets that still makes it one of the richest heritage towns in South India.

The star is Gol Gumbaz, the mausoleum of Mohammed Adil Shah, whose 44 m dome is among the largest unsupported domes in the world. Nearby, Ibrahim Rauza is often called the Taj Mahal of the Deccan. Don't miss the Jama Masjid, Asar Mahal, and Malik-e-Maidan — 'master of the field' — one of the largest medieval cannons in the world. Leave time for the bazaars, too.

places.name: Gol Gumbaz
places.summary: Mohammed Adil Shah's 210 ft mausoleum with a vast dome and an echoing whispering gallery; open 10 am–5 pm.
places.seoTitle: Gol Gumbaz, Vijayapura — the whispering gallery
places.seoDescription: Gol Gumbaz, Vijayapura: a 210 ft mausoleum with one of the world's largest domes and a whispering gallery that echoes 10–11 times. Open 10 am–5 pm.

images.alt: Gol Gumbaz's white walls, seven-storey corner towers and great dome
images.caption: Gol Gumbaz

overview.text:
Gol Gumbaz is the mausoleum of Sultan Mohammed Adil Shah and the landmark of Vijayapura. It rises 210 feet, with an octagonal seven-storey tower at each corner and, on top, a vast dome — second in size only to St Peter's Basilica in Rome. It took two decades to build.

The great experience is inside the dome. Climb the narrow stairs in one of the towers to the whispering gallery that runs around its base: the acoustics are so strong that a sound echoes 10 to 11 times, and a whisper on one side can be heard on the other. Go early, before the crowds, to hear it properly. The monument is open from 10 am to 5 pm, and sits within a complex of other historic buildings.

items.body: 10 am–5 pm

items.body: 210 ft

places.seoDescription: Ibrahim Rauza: the 'Taj Mahal of the Deccan', tomb of Ibrahim Adil Shah II and his queen, with a mosque across a terrace of pools. Open 6 am–6 pm.

images.alt: Ibrahim Rauza's tomb and mosque facing each other across a lawn
images.caption: Ibrahim Rauza

overview.text:
Ibrahim Rauza is often called the Taj Mahal of the Deccan, and it is a love story in stone: the mausoleum of Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II and his queen. Built of limestone and dark basalt, it blends Hindu and Islamic artistic traditions in its fine carving and perfect proportions.

The complex sits on a raised stone terrace. The tomb stands to the east and a mosque to the west, facing each other across a podium broken by fountains and still ornamental pools. Walk slowly around both to take in the carved screens, domes and minarets, then step inside the tomb chamber with its curved ceiling panels. It is open from 6 am to 6 pm; the soft light of early morning or late afternoon suits it best.

places.name: Bidar
places.summary: The 'City of Whispering Monuments' in Karnataka's far north — Bahmani fort, tombs and the Nanak Jhira gurudwara.
places.seoTitle: Bidar — fort, Bahmani tombs and Nanak Jhira Sahib
places.seoDescription: Bidar: the Bahmani-era Bidar Fort, Bahmani Tombs and Gurudwara Nanak Jhira Sahib, in Karnataka's far north.

images.alt: Bidar Fort's walls and palaces among gardens
images.caption: Bidar Fort

overview.text:
Bidar, in the far north of Karnataka, is known as the City of Whispering Monuments. Its history runs back more than two thousand years, but its great age came with the Bahmani Sultanate, which built the vast fort that still dominates the town in the 14th century.

Inside the walls are palaces such as Rangin Mahal; outside, the domed Bahmani Tombs stand in their own quiet grounds. Bidar is also a place of pilgrimage: Gurudwara Nanak Jhira Sahib honours the visit of Guru Nanak Dev Ji. Leave time for the markets, which sell local handicrafts, textiles and souvenirs. It makes a rewarding, uncrowded stop for anyone exploring the Deccan's Islamic heritage.

places.name: Bidar Fort
places.summary: The Bahmani capital's great fort — 37 bastions and 30-plus palaces and mosques, 2.5 km from the station.
places.seoDescription: Bidar Fort: Bahmani capital from 1430, 37 octagonal bastions, Rangin Mahal, Gagan Mahal and Takhat Mahal; 2.5 km from Bidar station.

images.commons: File:Gumbaz Darwaza in the Bidar fort.jpg
images.alt: The red stone Gumbaz Darwaza gateway of Bidar Fort
images.caption: Gumbaz Darwaza, Bidar Fort

overview.text:
Bidar Fort is one of the great forts of the Deccan, built in the Persian style. A stronghold stood here under the Western Chalukyas, but its present form dates from 1430, when Sultan Ahmed Shah Wali of the Bahmani dynasty made Bidar his capital and rebuilt it on a grand scale.

Its defences are formidable: 37 massive octagonal bastions — the Munda Burj is the most impressive — once armed with cannons. Inside the walls are more than 30 Islamic buildings, among them Rangin Mahal with its tilework, Gagan Mahal and Takhat Mahal. Enter through the red stone Gumbaz Darwaza and allow a few hours to explore. The fort is only 2.5 km from Bidar railway station.

items.body: 2.5 km

places.name: Chikkamagaluru (Chikmagalur)
places.summary: Karnataka's coffee hills — estates, rainforest and the state's highest peak, 240 km from Bengaluru.
places.seoDescription: Chikkamagaluru: coffee estates, Baba Budangiri where coffee came to India, and Mullayanagiri, Karnataka's highest peak. 240 km from Bengaluru.

images.alt: Cloud filling the valleys below green hills near Chikkamagaluru
images.caption: Hills near Chikkamagaluru

overview.text:
Chikkamagaluru — usually called Chikmagalur — sits in the foothills of the Chandra Drona range of the Western Ghats and is Karnataka's coffee country. Visitors come for its pleasant hill-station climate, rainforest and coffee estates.

This is where coffee's Indian story begins: on Baba Budangiri, the hills to the north, the saint Baba Budan is believed to have planted the first coffee in India. The same range holds Mullayanagiri, the highest peak in Karnataka, and the drive up gives some of the best views in the Ghats. The town is about 240 km from Bengaluru and 183 km from Mysuru. Winters are cool, at about 11–20 °C; summers reach 25–32 °C.

places.name: Mullayanagiri
places.summary: Karnataka's highest peak, 1,925 m, with a small summit temple above Chikkamagaluru.
places.seoDescription: Mullayanagiri: at 1,925 m Karnataka's highest peak, near Chikkamagaluru, with a small summit temple and wide Western Ghats views.

images.alt: The grassy summit ridge of Mullayanagiri
images.caption: Mullayanagiri

overview.text:
Mullayanagiri is the highest peak in Karnataka, at 1,925 m (6,316 ft), rising from the Baba Budangiri range above Chikkamagaluru. Grassy ridges fall away on every side, and on a clear day the view reaches across the Western Ghats; in the monsoon, cloud races over the summit.

At the top is a small temple dedicated to the sage Mullappa Swamy, who gave the peak its name. He is believed to have meditated in the shallow caves just below the summit. A road climbs most of the way, then a flight of steps leads to the top; trekkers also follow the older trail along the ridge. Go early for the clearest views, and take a layer — it is often windy and cool up here.

items.body: Mullappa Swamy temple

places.name: Chennakeshava Temple, Belur
places.summary: The 1117 Hoysala masterpiece at Belur, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023 — still a living Vishnu temple.
places.seoDescription: Belur's Chennakeshava Temple: commissioned 1117, 103 years in the making, part of UNESCO's Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas. 35 km from Hassan.

images.alt: The intricately carved Chennakeshava Temple at Belur
images.caption: Chennakeshava Temple, Belur

overview.text:
The Chennakeshava Temple at Belur is one of the masterpieces of Hoysala art. King Vishnuvardhana commissioned it in 1117 on the banks of the Yagachi river, in what was then an early Hoysala capital, and it took three generations — 103 years — to finish. Damaged and rebuilt many times, it has remained a living temple to Vishnu ever since.

The carving is extraordinary: friezes of elephants, dancers and scenes from the epics wrap the star-shaped walls, and bracket figures of graceful dancers lean from the pillars. In 2023, Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site as the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas. Belur is 35 km from Hassan and about 220 km from Bengaluru; Halebidu is 15 km away.

places.name: Halebidu
places.summary: The old Hoysala capital — the Hoysalesvara temple, Jain basadis and a stepwell, 15 km from Belur.
places.seoDescription: Halebidu, the old Hoysala capital Dvarasamudra: the Hoysalesvara and Kedareshwara temples, Jain basadis, the Hulikere stepwell. 15 km from Belur.

images.alt: The twin-shrined Hoysalesvara temple at Halebidu
images.caption: Hoysalesvara temple, Halebidu

overview.text:
Halebidu — the name means "old capital" — was Dvarasamudra, the royal capital of the Hoysala Empire from the 11th century. Today it is a quiet village, but its temples hold some of the finest Hindu and Jain carving in India.

The great sight is the Hoysalesvara temple, its walls covered in bands of elephants, lions, scrolls and scenes from the epics, with hundreds of gods and dancers above. Nearby are the Kedareshwara temple, a group of Jain basadis, and the Hulikere stepwell. Together with Belur and Somanathapura, the Hoysala temples here are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Halebidu is 30 km from Hassan, 150 km from Mysuru and about 15 km from Belur, so the two are easily seen in one day.

places.name: Shravanabelagola
places.summary: The great Jain pilgrimage town — the 57-ft Gommateshwara statue on Vindhyagiri, 144 km from Bengaluru.
places.seoDescription: Shravanabelagola: the 57-ft monolithic Gommateshwara Bahubali on Vindhyagiri, Chandragiri's basadis and the 12-yearly Mahamastakabhisheka (next 2030).

images.alt: The giant monolithic statue of Gommateshwara Bahubali
images.caption: Gommateshwara, Shravanabelagola

overview.text:
Shravanabelagola, between two granite hills in Hassan district, is one of the most important pilgrimage places in Jainism. On Vindhyagiri stands the 57-ft monolithic statue of Gommateshwara Bahubali, carved from a single rock, gazing calmly over the plains. It is reached by a long flight of steps cut into the hill.

Across the town, Chandragiri hill is crowded with old basadis and inscriptions; tradition says the emperor Chandragupta Maurya died here as a Jain monk in 298 BCE. Every twelve years the statue is anointed with water, milk, turmeric, sandalwood and flowers in the Mahamastakabhisheka — the last was in February 2018 and the next is due in 2030. The town is 144 km from Bengaluru and 83 km from Mysuru.

places.name: Keshava Temple, Somanathapura
places.summary: A perfect 13th-century Hoysala temple near Mysuru, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site; open 9 am–5:30 pm.
places.seoDescription: Somanathapura's Keshava Temple: 13th-century Hoysala, three star-shaped shrines, UNESCO 2023. Open 9 am–5:30 pm; best October–March.

images.alt: The three star-shaped towers of the Keshava Temple at Somanathapura
images.caption: Keshava Temple, Somanathapura

overview.text:
The Keshava Temple at Somanathapura is the most complete and perfectly preserved of the Hoysala temples. It was built in the 13th century, in the reign of King Narasimha III, and stands in a walled courtyard ringed by a pillared cloister.

Three star-shaped shrines rise from a single raised platform, every surface covered in carving — bands of elephants, horsemen and scrolls at the base, and panels of gods and goddesses above. Walk slowly around the outside to read the friezes. Since 2023 it has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, together with Belur and Halebidu. It is open from 9 am to 5:30 pm, and October to March, the cooler months, is the best time to visit. It makes an easy half-day trip from Mysuru.

places.name: Talakaveri
places.summary: The sacred source of the Kaveri in Coorg's Brahmagiri hills, 48 km from Madikeri.
places.seoTitle: Talakaveri — source of the Kaveri, Coorg
places.seoDescription: Talakaveri, 48 km from Madikeri at 1,276 m in the Brahmagiri hills: the sacred source of the Kaveri. Best October–March.

images.alt: Talakaveri's temple and hills of the Brahmagiri range
images.caption: Talakaveri

overview.text:
Talakaveri, high in the Brahmagiri hills of Coorg, is revered as the source of the Kaveri, one of the most sacred rivers of South India. It lies at about 1,276 m in the Western Ghats, and pilgrims come to the small tank where the river is said to rise.

Around the shrine, steps climb the hillside to a viewpoint over rolling green ridges that stretch towards Kerala; on clear days it is one of the finest views in Coorg. Go between October and March, when the weather is clear for sightseeing and walks. Talakaveri is about 48 km from Madikeri by road; the nearest airport is Kannur, about 120 km away, and the nearest major railway station is Mysuru.

places.name: Dandeli
places.summary: Karnataka's hornbill forest on the Kali river — elephants, tigers, 300+ birds; open 9 am–6 pm.
places.seoTitle: Dandeli National Park and the Kali river
places.seoDescription: Dandeli: Western Ghats forest on the Kali river with elephants, tigers in the Kali Tiger Reserve and 300+ birds, including three hornbills. Open 9 am–6 pm.

images.commons: File:A silent scene of kali river dandeli, india.jpg
images.alt: The still Kali river through forest at Dandeli
images.caption: The Kali river, Dandeli

overview.text:
Dandeli lies in the evergreen forests of the Western Ghats, along the Kali river, and is one of Karnataka's great wild places. Its mix of river, thick forest and hills shelters an impressive list of animals: the Dandeli Elephant Reserve holds more than 60 elephants under Project Elephant, tigers are seen in the Dandeli (Kali) Tiger Reserve, and leopards slip through the hills.

For birdwatchers it is a dream: more than 300 species have been recorded, and Malabar pied, Indian grey and great hornbills are commonly seen along the river and in the tall timber forest. Look out too for Malabar giant squirrels and smooth-coated otters. The park is open from 9 am to 6 pm.

items.body: 9 am–6 pm

items.title: Birds

places.name: Bandipur National Park
places.summary: 1,456 sq km of tiger and elephant forest on the Mysuru–Ooty road, a tiger reserve since 1973.
places.seoDescription: Bandipur: 1,456 sq km in Chamarajanagar, a Project Tiger reserve since 1973 — elephants, tigers, gaur, sloth bears and dholes.

images.alt: A wild elephant in the forest at Bandipur
images.caption: Elephant, Bandipur

overview.text:
Bandipur National Park covers 1,456 sq km of forest in Chamarajanagar district, in the far south of Karnataka. It began in 1931 as the Maharaja of Mysore's 90 sq km Venugopala Wildlife Park and became a tiger reserve under Project Tiger in 1973, when nearly 800 sq km were added.

It is one of the best places in India to see wild Asian elephants. Tigers, gaur, sloth bears, four-horned antelope, golden jackals and dholes — wild dogs — also live here, and even from the public roads through the park you are likely to see chital, grey langurs, Indian giant squirrels and elephants. Drive carefully and never stop to feed animals; collisions with vehicles are a real danger to wildlife here.
